title: Gear, Controls & Inspection
summary: What protective gear to wear, how to get to know a motorcycle and its controls, and how to check it with T-CLOCS before every ride.

blocks.text: In any crash, you have the best chance of avoiding serious injury if you wear three things: a DOT-compliant helmet, face or eye protection, and protective clothing.

rows: About 1 in every 5 motorcycle crashes causes one. Together they make up most serious and fatal rider injuries, and head injuries are far more common than neck injuries.
Most happen on short trips (under 5 miles), just a few minutes after starting out.
Most riders are going slower than 30 mph. At these speeds a helmet can cut the number and severity of head and neck injuries by about half.
At any speed, riders wearing helmets are 3 times more likely to survive head injuries.

blocks.text: Some riders worry that a helmet blocks their view. It does not: a DOT-compliant helmet lets you see as far to the sides as you need, and studies show it does not keep you from spotting danger.
The single most important thing you can do to improve your chances in a crash is to wear a quality helmet that is securely fastened.
The manual recommends two main helmet styles, each with a different level of coverage: three-quarter and full face. Whichever you choose, make sure the helmet:

items: Meets U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) and state standards. A Snell Memorial Foundation label is an extra sign of quality.
Fits snugly, all the way around your head.
Has no obvious defects, such as cracks, loose padding or frayed straps.

blocks.text: Fasten the strap every time you ride. An unfastened helmet can fly off in a crash before it has a chance to protect you.

items: A plastic, impact-resistant faceshield helps protect your whole face. It also blocks wind, dust, rain, insects and pebbles thrown up by cars.
Goggles protect your eyes, but not the rest of your face.
A windshield is not a substitute for a faceshield or goggles. Most windshields will not protect your eyes from the wind.
Eyeglasses and sunglasses are not enough either. They do not stop watering eyes and can blow off.

blocks.text: To do its job, eye or face protection must:

items: Be free of scratches.
Resist penetration.
Give a clear view to both sides.
Fasten securely so it does not blow off.
Let air pass through to reduce fogging.
Leave room for eyeglasses or sunglasses, if needed.

blocks.text: Do not wear tinted eye protection when there is little light, such as at dusk or night. Switch to clear protection instead of riding without any.

rows: Cover arms and legs completely. Snug enough not to flap in the wind, loose enough to move freely. Leather protects best; sturdy synthetic material also protects well.
Still wear a jacket. It helps prevent dehydration, and many are made to protect without overheating you.
High and sturdy enough to cover and support your ankles. Soles should be hard, durable and slip-resistant.
Keep heels short so they do not catch on rough surfaces. Tuck in laces so they do not catch on the motorcycle.
Made of leather or a similar durable material. They give a better grip and protect your hands.
Long-term engine and wind noise can cause permanent hearing damage, even under a full-face helmet. Good protection cuts noise but still lets you hear horns and sirens.

blocks.text: In cold or wet weather, dress to stay warm and dry. You cannot control a motorcycle well if you are numb, and long rides in the cold cause severe chill and fatigue. A winter jacket should block wind and fit snugly at the neck, wrists and waist.
Rules about hearing protection vary. Check your state's rule in the State Cheat Sheet.

items: It should fit you: your feet reach the ground while you are seated, and the controls are easy to operate.
Smaller motorcycles are usually easier for beginners.
Read the owner's manual. It is the main source for how your motorcycle should be inspected and maintained, including the regular upkeep schedule.
Avoid add-ons and modifications that make the motorcycle harder to handle.

blocks.text: At a minimum, a street-legal motorcycle should have:

items: Headlight, taillight and brake light
Front and rear brakes
Turn signals
Horn
Two mirrors

blocks.text: A wobble is when the front wheel and handlebars suddenly shake from side to side. Most wobbles come from improper loading, unsuitable accessories or incorrect tire pressure. Lighten or reposition heavy loads and make sure windshields and fairings are mounted properly.

rows: Squeeze the lever on the right handgrip
Squeeze the lever on the left handgrip
Lever in front of the left footrest, worked by the left foot
Pedal pressed with the right foot

blocks.text: Riding a new or borrowed motorcycle adds risk. More than half of all crashes involve riders with less than five months of experience on their motorcycle. Before riding an unfamiliar bike:

items: Read its owner's manual and get familiar with it away from traffic.
Learn where the turn signals, horn, headlight switch, fuel-supply valve and engine cut-off switch are, so you can use them without looking.
Work the throttle, clutch lever, brakes and shifter a few times before you ride. On a manual transmission, get very familiar with the clutch's friction zone.
Ride very carefully at first: accelerate gently, take turns more slowly and leave extra room for stopping.

blocks.text: If you lend your motorcycle, make sure your friend is licensed and knows how to ride before they head into traffic.
A motorcycle needs more frequent attention than a car, because a small failure can cause a crash. A T-CLOCS check takes only a few minutes and should be done before every ride.

rows: Check tire pressure (when tires are cold, adjusted to your load), tread wear and sidewalls. Try each brake alone: it should feel firm and hold the motorcycle.
Clutch and throttle work smoothly. The throttle snaps back to fully closed when released and the engine does not rev when you turn the handlebars. The horn works.
Headlight (high and low beam), taillight and all turn signals work. Each brake turns on the brake light. Clean and adjust mirrors.
Check engine oil and transmission fluid. Check brake fluid and coolant (if equipped) weekly. Open the fuel valve. Look under the bike for leaks.
Suspension moves smoothly with no binding. Chain or belt adjusted to the maker's specs; sprockets not worn or damaged.
Side stand moves smoothly and its spring holds it firmly up. A center stand stays tight against the frame while moving.

items: Mirrors: adjust before you start, not while riding. Each should show the lane behind you and the lane next to you. Seeing the edge of your arm or shoulder is fine.
Engine oil: check it warm, on the center stand, on level ground, using the dipstick or sight glass. Check coolant only when the engine is cool.
Fuel valve: if it is closed, the bike may start on fuel left in the lines, then stall once the lines are empty.

blocks.text: A throttle that sticks or revs the engine when you turn the handlebars is a serious hazard. Fix it before you ride.

keyPoints: Wear a DOT-compliant helmet, face or eye protection, and protective clothing on every ride, even short ones.
Wearing a securely fastened, quality helmet is the single most important thing you can do to improve your chances in a crash; helmeted riders are 3 times more likely to survive head injuries.
A windshield or sunglasses do not replace a faceshield or goggles, and tinted protection is unsafe in low light.
Choose sturdy clothing that covers you fully: leather or strong synthetics, gloves, and boots that cover your ankles.
A motorcycle should fit you, and a street-legal one needs lights, both brakes, turn signals, a horn and two mirrors.
Throttle and front brake are on the right handgrip, clutch on the left; left foot shifts, right foot works the rear brake.
Get familiar with any new or borrowed bike away from traffic and ride it cautiously.
Do a T-CLOCS check before every ride: Tires and wheels, Controls, Lights and electrics, Oil and fluids, Chassis, Stands.
